claims.text: Adding approximately 5 at.% Mo to a Ti- and Ni-rich single-phase solid-solution HEA will improve its elevated-temperature mechanical properties.
The initial alloy is a single-phase solid solution in which Ti and Ni are primary constituents.
The intervention is to add approximately 5 at.% Mo during synthesis.
A 5 at.% Mo addition constitutes a major part of the composition rather than a trace addition.
The relevant test window is approximately 800–1200 °C under an inert or otherwise controlled atmosphere.
Mo will promote microstructural refinement through enhanced solid-solution and precipitation strengthening.
Mo may cause coherent nanoscale precipitates to form.
Mo will reduce grain-boundary mobility and thereby retard grain growth and impurity-induced softening at elevated temperature.
Mo raises the alloy's effective melting point, strengthens atomic bonding, and consequently increases lattice stability.
Mo-derived solid-solution strengthening and fine precipitates impede dislocation motion and grain-boundary sliding at elevated temperature.
Mo may scavenge oxygen or nitrogen interstitials that would otherwise promote local compositional fluctuations.
Interstitial oxygen and nitrogen can facilitate nanoscale phase segregation and reduce solid-solution strengthening during aging.
The Mo-modified alloy will have higher yield strength, lower creep rate, and better mechanical stability than the unmodified alloy.
The unmodified Ti–Ni-based HEA will have lower elevated-temperature strength and will soften during extended thermal exposure.
The beneficial effect of Mo is limited to concentrations below those that induce detrimental secondary phases.
Controlling impurities is important for maintaining the high-temperature stability of refractory HEAs.
The optimal Mo concentration and its roles in precipitation and impurity control in the proposed Ti–Ni-rich alloy are not established.

A controlled comparison of otherwise identically processed alloys, with and without approximately 5 at.% Mo, can falsify the hypothesis if the modified alloy lacks a statistically significant improvement, including at least 10% higher yield strength, or forms mechanically detrimental secondary phases.

contradictions.description: The Mo addition is described as both a small or minor addition and, at the same nominal concentration of about 5 at.%, a major part of the composition.

The applicability boundary says the alloy is maintained as a single-phase solid solution, while the proposed mediator invokes formation of coherent precipitates, which would make the modified microstructure multiphase unless the single-phase condition applies only before intervention.
